1) The standard pattern of intutions (bystander > footbridge) is preserved across domains and severity of harm; 2) The difference in intuitions between scenarios is greater for physical harms (injury/death) than non-physical harms; 3) The standard pattern is preserved for both types of harm.
the difference in judgements between the bystander and foot-bridge scenarios is replicated when the harms are economic and emotional rather than physical, and when the harms are injury and death.

(a) the standard pattern of moral intuitions in trolley dilemmas is preserved across domains of harm and across different levels of physical and economic harm, but not emotional harm, and (b) this pattern is preserved even when the harm to the victim is death.

the question of whether the same moral principles and psychological principles apply to harms that are not deaths.
the question of whether there is a moral principle underlying the moral intuitions of bystander and foot bridge scenarios.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the difference in intuitions between footbridge and bystander scenarios is robust across different domains of harm and different severity of harms.
there are no significant differences in moral judgements between the bystander and foot-bridge trolley problems across a wide range of domains and levels of severity of physical and nonphysical harm.
the bystander/footbridge difference is robust and that the moral principles underlying it are not specific to the domain or severity of harm, but apply to all harms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the bystander and the footbridge scenarios elicit different moral judgements in trolley dilemmas, and this difference is preserved across different domains and different levels of severity of the harm.
moral intuitions about trolley problems are not limited to the domain of physical harm.
there is no evidence that the moral principles and processes are limited to death.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the trolley problem is not just a thought experiment but a real-life dilemma.
the moral principles underlying trolley problems are not limited to death.
the moral principles and decision-making processes underlying trolley problems are not restricted to physical harms, but extend to economic and emotional harm as well.
